## Isaiah 7: Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- The coalition of Syria (Aram) and Israel and its failed attack are also recorded in 2 Kings 16. Isaiah tells us the outcome (they "could not prevail") before he describes his message to Ahaz. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-7/
- Background: Israel under Menahem was already paying tribute to Assyria. Pekah (called a usurper) and Rezin allied to resist Assyria, and Syria seems to have led. 2 Chronicles 28 reports a heavy defeat for Judah. Jerusalem was besieged but not taken, and Rezin captured the port of Elath. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/7.htm
- Jerusalem may have held out because it was strong, or because the attackers heard Assyria was threatening their own lands and couldn't keep up a long siege (Barnes). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-1.html
- God kept Jerusalem safe despite Ahaz's unfaithfulness. Replacing Ahaz would have ended the line of David, from which the Messiah was to come. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_7_commentary
- Ahaz's godly father and grandfather are named because Isaiah prophesied during their reigns. Gill rejects the Jewish view that the city was spared because of their merit. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm

**v. 2**
- "Ephraim" is another name for the northern kingdom of Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-7/
- "House of David" means Ahaz, his family, the princes and his advisers. "Aram is in league" is also translated "Syria led its army into Ephraim" or "rests upon Ephraim." The image is of a strong wind against weak trees. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- Each king alone had already hurt Ahaz badly, so a joint attack was frightening. It isn't clear whether Ahaz had asked Assyria for help yet. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm

**v. 3**
- Shear-jashub means "a remnant shall return," a return both physical and spiritual (that is, conversion). Ellicott thinks the boy was probably 16 to 18. Ahaz was probably overseeing siege defences and cutting off water outside the walls, as Hezekiah later did. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- The boy was probably brought along because of his name, to catch Ahaz's attention. The same aqueduct appears in 2 Kings 18:17. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm
- The Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) takes the "son" to mean Isaiah's disciples. The Launderer's Field was where cloth was washed and whitened. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-3.html
- The aqueduct ran above ground and could be attacked (Constable). — same URL
- The name was meant to encourage captives that a remnant would return (Matthew Henry). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_007.cfm

**v. 4**
- The right attitude was calm courage and waiting on the Lord (compare Isaiah 30:15). "Disheartened" is literally "let not your heart be soft." The two kings are like torch stumps whose flame is almost out. Calling Pekah only "son of Remaliah" is a put-down, like "son of Jesse" for David. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- The "smoldering stubs" show how weak the kings are and how short their anger will last. Their fury is like smoke about to vanish. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm

**v. 5**
- There are only two parties, not three. The Syrian king isn't named here and Pekah is named only by his father, both on purpose, to show contempt. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-7.html

**v. 6**
- "Make a breach" means attacking Judah's chain of fortresses. "Tabeal" is an Aramaic name meaning "good is God," which suggests a man of low birth, perhaps an officer in Rezin's army. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- "Terrorize" (KJV "vex") means to besiege or distress. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-7.html

**v. 7**
- "Lord GOD" is literally "Lord Jehovah." The plan to set aside David's line, which God had promised to keep (2 Samuel 7), was bound to fail. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-7.html
- What looked like an unstoppable plot was, from heaven's view, a fragile conspiracy against God's covenant. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_7_commentary

**v. 8**
- Syria and Ephraim have only human heads. Judah, by implication, has a divine Head. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-7.html
- Each kingdom will stay small and won't grow by conquering Judah. Ellicott calls the 65 years Isaiah's first dated prediction. Some critics (Ewald) thought the clause was added later. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/7.htm
- **The 65 years:** Samaria fell only about 18 or 19 years after this. Gill therefore follows the Targum and counts to the end of 65 years. That points to the reign of Esarhaddon, who resettled the land in Manasseh's 22nd year (following Prideaux). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- The prediction was fulfilled when Esarhaddon devastated the land and filled it with foreigners (Preacher's Homiletical Commentary). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-7.html
- The northern kingdom was gone within 65 years (Chuck Smith). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-14.html

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests "If ye will not hold this faith fast, surely ye will not stand fast." Full trust in v. 7 would have freed Ahaz from political schemes. His distrust led to moves that made him less secure (2 Kings 16:7–18; 2 Chronicles 28:16, 20). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm
- Lesson drawn: when faith fails, power goes. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-7.html
- W. E. Vine says difficulties encourage and strengthen faith. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_7_commentary
- Ellicott thinks Ahaz didn't believe a promise he wouldn't live to see fulfilled. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html

**v. 10**
- There's no need to assume a time gap before this verse (against Cheyne). The first message seems to have been met with silence, so God gives Ahaz another chance. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm

**v. 11**
- Gideon asked for a sign and received it. When God himself offers one and lets you choose, accepting is not wrong. "Depths or heights" means any sign at all, from the grave to heaven. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm
- God is still "your God" to wicked Ahaz, as God of the nation. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm

**v. 12**
- Ahaz had already decided to turn to Assyria and may already have sent envoys. He hid behind the law against testing God (Deuteronomy 6:16). It was false humility: he took a humble posture but did not obey. Unlike the Pharisees, who demanded signs, Ahaz refused one that God offered. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-7.html
- He claimed to be religious and reverent, but refusing a sign God had offered can't be called testing God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- Refusing was a deliberate provocation that treated grace with contempt. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_7_commentary

**v. 13**
- Note the shift from "the LORD your God" (v. 11) to "my God." Trying God's patience is a typical Isaiah theme (1:14). Speaking to the whole "house of David" may mean older royals backed Ahaz's Assyrian plan. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- The Targum reads "weary men" as wearing out the prophets. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- Isaiah gladly calls God "my God," which Ahaz would not do (Matthew Henry). — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-14.html

**v. 14** (the main point of disagreement)
- **Near and far fulfilment (Guzik, Enduring Word):** There is a near fulfilment for Ahaz, that within a few years Syria and Israel would be crushed, and a far fulfilment in Jesus. "The virgin shall conceive" and a sign to the whole house of David point to Christ. — https://enduringword.com/promise-near-far/ ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-7/
- **Directly about Christ (Calvin, Reformed):** Calvin doesn't argue over the word. Even if *almah* sometimes means "young woman," what wonder would a normal pregnancy be? — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-14.html
- **Directly about Christ (Gill, Baptist):**
  - Gill says *almah* means a pure virgin wherever it appears, and the Septuagint's Jewish translators used "virgin."
  - Isaiah's wife already had children and couldn't be called a virgin.
  - The sign is the Messiah, born far in the future yet a pledge of present rescue: Judah couldn't cease to exist before he came.
  - Sources: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-7.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- **Two views laid out (Ellicott):**
  - *View 1:* Isaiah points to some young woman of his day, and "Immanuel" is a name that rebukes the faithless king, not a statement that God became man.
  - *View 2:* Matthew 1:23 settles it, and Isaiah saw "the virgin mother" in a vision.
  - *Problems with View 2:* How could a far-off birth be a sign to Ahaz? And no later prophet or Jewish interpreter cites a virgin birth as a mark of the Messiah.
  - *His conclusion:* Matthew, perhaps helped by the Septuagint's word, found a meaning Isaiah may not have fully grasped. The prophecy has "springing and germinant accomplishments," and Christ is the "ultimate and true Immanuel."
  - Source: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/7.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Rejects the idea that the mother is Isaiah's wife. "The virgin" would be an odd title for her, and the rank given Immanuel in 8:8 doesn't fit Isaiah's son. It discusses Bishop Lowth's view of a double meaning: a woman who was a virgin then would conceive, and the enemies would fall within a few years. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm
- **Constable (Dallas evangelical):** *Almah* means a young woman of marriageable age and is never used of a married woman. Isaiah may have chosen it over *bethulah* ("virgin") to allow two fulfilments: first Isaiah's son Maher-shalal-hash-baz, later a virgin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-14.html
- **Coffman (Church of Christ):** Strongly insists on "virgin" and calls the RSV's "young woman" a betrayal of the faith. **Barnes:** The word means an unmarried girl of marriageable age, and it's used of Rebekah and Miriam. — same URL
- **Utley (bible.org):** The sign must first apply to Ahaz's day, especially given vv. 15–16. — https://bible.org/book/export/html/21138
- **The Gospel Coalition (Sinclair):** Answers the claim that the verse is "really about Hezekiah." The Jewish translators of the Septuagint used a word that clearly means "virgin." Old Testament prophecy is often "both/and": a young woman then, a virgin in the greater fulfilment. — https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-matthew-get-isaiahs-prophecy-of-the-virgin-birth-wrong/
- **GotQuestions:** *Almah* basically means "young woman." None of its seven uses requires "virgin," and none rules it out. Neither side can prove its case, but the Septuagint's *parthenos* makes "virgin" likely. — https://www.gotquestions.org/virgin-or-young-woman.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):**
  - The NET translates "this young woman is about to conceive." It says *almah* doesn't in itself mean virgin, and related words in Aramaic and Ugaritic are used of women who weren't virgins.
  - The woman was probably present at the scene, perhaps a member of the royal family.
  - Sources: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Isa+7%3A14%2C19 ; https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=isa+7:10-17
- **Catholic:**
  - The "just another royal son" reading is absurd. Ahaz already had sons (he burned some as offerings, 2 Chronicles 28:3), and a sign "deep as Sheol or high as heaven" points to the child of 9:6, called "Mighty God." — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/virgin-birth
  - The Septuagint shows that "virgin" was the accepted meaning centuries before Christ. — https://www.catholic.com/qa/does-the-bible-prophecy-say-that-the-mother-of-the-messiah-would-be-a-virgin-or-only-a-young
  - A more cautious Catholic answer (citing John Watts): *almah* only sometimes means a virgin. Prophecy works on more than one level, and the greater fulfilment came long after Ahaz. — https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/a-virgin-shall-conceive
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says only that Emmanuel means "God with us" and is the child foretold in Isaiah 7:14. It notes that views on who the child is vary. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05404a.htm

**v. 15**
- **Messianic reading (Gill):** Jesus ate such food because he was born in a land of milk and honey during a peaceful, plentiful time. The phrase also shows he was truly human. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/7.htm
- **Hardship reading (Ellicott):** With fields abandoned, people hiding in caves would live on nomads' food. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- **Grammar (NET):** "By the time He knows" is literally "for his knowing." In the other 40 uses of this construction it shows purpose or result, not time. — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=isa+7:10-17

**v. 16**
- The phrase points to an age approaching manhood, by which time Pekah and Rezin will have fallen. "Reject evil and choose good" refers to moral choice, not just telling good food from bad. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- The near meaning is that both kings would be gone within about twelve years (Chuck Smith). Bridgeway puts it at two or three years. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-1.html
- Timing is essential to a prophecy built on the word "before." The Pulpit Commentary rejects Cheyne's idea that Isaiah expected the Messiah to come during the Assyrian invasion. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-7.html

**v. 17**
- Assyria, the nation Ahaz trusted, would bring ruin. What looked like a clever move would turn out terribly. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-7/
- Ahaz is bringing on an invasion worse than any since the kingdom split, including Shishak's under Rehoboam. Isaiah saves the words "king of Assyria" for the end, for effect. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- "Since Ephraim separated" means since Jeroboam's revolt (1 Kings 12). The sudden turn from promise to threat should have shaken Ahaz. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- The Egyptian "fly" and the Assyrian "bee" stand for their armies. From Sargon to Cyrus, Judah was the battleground between them. This may include Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo (2 Kings 23). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/7.htm
- Compare Isaiah 5:26, where God whistles for a distant nation. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_7_commentary

**v. 20**
- "Hired razor" refers to the tribute Ahaz would pay Tiglath-pileser. Compare 2 Chronicles 28:19. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html

**vv. 21–22**
- "Two sheep" is better "two ewes." Herds once counted in thousands are now counted singly. "Abundance" is ironic, because there are so few people left. "Curds and honey" darkly echoes the "land of milk and honey." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-7.html
- Calvin: so few people remain that a little milk is enough. He reads this as a threat, not a promise. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-7.html

**vv. 23–25**
- Bridgeway's summary of the passage as a whole: farmland would be ruined, and people would depend on animals and insects for food. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/7-1.html
- (Ellicott's note on v. 23 was cut off, and I found nothing else on these verses.)

---

**Where traditions differ, in summary:** The real disagreement is v. 14, with v. 15 following from it.
- **Christ only:** Calvin and Gill read it as directly and only about Christ, as do Coffman and the Catholic Answers magazine piece.
- **Near and far:** Enduring Word, TGC, Constable, Chuck Smith and the cautious Catholic answer see a near fulfilment plus a far one.
- **A meaning Isaiah may not have grasped:** Ellicott leans toward a fuller meaning that Matthew drew out.
- **Young woman of Isaiah's day:** The NET notes read it this way in its original setting.
